result.question: Research the concrete, nameable "tells" that reveal a website was AI-generated or built from a template rather than custom-designed — for PIIIX-org/portfolio.me, an agent-run pipeline whose premise is that two runs must never look alike. Cover: (1) named AI-generation tells (gradient heroes, "safe" typefaces, bento grids, emoji bullets, rigid grid-column allegiance, etc.), (2) template tells distinct from AI tells (component fingerprints, boilerplate section order), (3) grid systems and the named-practitioner discourse on deliberately breaking a grid vs. rigid submission to it, (4) named critics/juries on homogenized or "AI slop" web design (re-verifying Kyle Chayka's actual claims), and (5) UI/UX rules and when experts deliberately break them. Every claim must trace to a named, identifiable source actually making that observation (practitioner, critic, studio, jury, newsroom) — Tier B opinion is admissible and expected; refute only if the source doesn't say it, says something different, or is unsourced/anonymous.
result.summary: This is a retry of a gap that failed twice under an abstract framing ("named critics on distinctive vs homogenized design"); the fix is to hunt for concrete, individually-checkable claims (a specific pattern + a specific named source saying it's a tell) rather than movements or schools of thought. The six angles split cleanly across the five required areas, with one angle dedicated specifically to stress-testing the hypothesized "rigid grid-column allegiance" tell (the example most likely to have zero real source behind it) separately from the general grid-breaking discourse, and one angle dedicated to re-verifying Kyle Chayka's exact wording rather than trusting the prior pass's paraphrase.
